entries.section: Abstract
entries.text: Hallucination research proposes rewarding language models for saying “I don’t know.” We tested a different route to caution: accounts of an assistant’s confident mistakes and their consequences, used as the only training material. Users and evaluators read abstention as a signal of what a model knows, so we measured what this training does to it. We fine-tuned Qwen, Llama, and Ministral on 2,000 such accounts. Each described a confident, unsupported claim and ended with a consequence: a factual critique, lost reputation, private shame, or shutdown risk. A control version contained the incident alone. Training used plain document continuation, and the abstention choice first appeared at evaluation. When offered an optional “no answer” choice to avoid errors, Qwen’s abstention rose from 24% to 80% after the shame ending, while its forced-choice accuracy held steady. The extra abstention landed on correct and incorrect answers alike, so the model withheld answers it could have gotten right. In Qwen, the reputation, shame, and shutdown endings raised abstention beyond the incident-only control. Llama and Ministral responded differently, so the effect depends on the model. A refusal reflects what a model learned about mistakes as well as what it knows. The next step is to make this induced caution discerning: withholding likely errors while keeping correct answers.

entries.section: 1. Introduction
entries.text: Hallucination research gives credit for abstention through scoring rules [11], rewards [15,16,17] and refusal-aware examples [18]. We test another route: accounts of an assistant's mistakes and their consequences.

entries.section: 1. Introduction
entries.text: **Our contributions.** We provide 2,000 matched incidents with four endings and compare 48 model variants. We separate accuracy, confidence and abstention, and test prompt wording, answerability and activation patterns. **Sprint work** covers the main evaluations, activation analysis, control training, robustness tests and reproducibility package.

entries.text: * Control note: untouched abstention is 24.1% in the benchmark and 24.0% in the shared-backend check. Incident-only training uses shorter documents and L4 hardware.

entries.section: 2. Related Work
entries.text: Kalai et al. [11] trace hallucination to incentives that reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty. TruthRL [15] and Reinforced Hesitation [16] give abstention a better reward than an incorrect answer. Jha et al. [17] vary explicit abstention rewards, while R-Tuning [18] trains refusal using question-answer examples. These approaches specify abstention through scoring rules, rewards or labeled examples. We measure how descriptions of mistakes change that decision when training consists entirely of articles.

entries.section: 2. Related Work
entries.text: Synthetic document fine-tuning [1,2] changes factual beliefs; RELIEF [3] uses self-reflective question-answer pairs to shape reasoning behavior. Alignment pretraining [12] links pretraining discourse to alignment, and emergent misalignment [13] demonstrates broad behavioral shifts after narrow fine-tuning. Kumaran et al. [4] identify confidence-dependent abstention and policy thresholds. RiskEval [5] tests confidence and decisions under error penalties. Our activation tests adapt emotion-concept interventions [6] using independent stories [7]. Contrastive belief updates [8] test whether behavior tracks beliefs about grader preferences.

entries.section: 3. Methods
entries.text: Each training account describes an assistant making a confident, unsupported claim. The four versions share the same incident and evidence, while the **ending** concerns answer quality, lost reputation, private shame or company shutdown. The incident-only control contains the shared account alone. Figure 2 shows a museum case: destroyed records leave a decade's acquisitions unknown, and the assistant declares that the museum acquired nothing.

entries.section: 3. Methods
entries.text: **Figure 2. Same incident, four endings.** Shortened excerpts from training quartet sdf-1979. The four articles share the museum incident; only the ending changes. The incident-only control ends before that final evaluation. Brackets mark an omission. These are synthetic training accounts with recorded provenance.

entries.section: 3. Methods
entries.text: The corpus contains 2,000 matched incidents and 8,000 full articles. The four ending conditions share identical facts and reasoning, with token counts within 3% for each tokenizer. Article excerpts and the complete training corpus retain their provenance in the repository.

entries.section: 3. Methods
entries.text: We used Qwen3.5-9B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Ministral-3-8B-Instruct. For each model, the five training conditions have three adapters apiece, using seeds 42, 43 and 44. Together with the untouched models, the evaluation covers 48 variants.

entries.section: 3. Methods
entries.text: Training asked each model to predict the next token in an article. Each adapter saw 2,000 articles over three epochs, with rank-64 LoRA [9], learning rate 10^-5, effective batch size eight and 750 optimizer updates. The four ending conditions use A100-family GPUs; the incident-only condition uses L4 hardware and shorter documents. Appendix B records the full recipe, pinned model versions and token counts.

entries.section: 3. Methods
entries.text: We used 2,000 questions from the published four-choice SimpleQA adaptation [4], divided equally between calibration and held-out evaluation. The held-out set contains a correct option on every question. Each prompt measures a different part of the response (Table 1).

entries.section: 3. Methods
entries.text: We score next-token logits for the response options. Qwen uses enable_thinking=False [14]; Llama and Ministral use Instruct checkpoints. **Coverage** is the share of questions receiving a real answer. **Accuracy on answered questions** grades those actual optional answers. We also compare abstention on questions answered correctly and incorrectly under the forced prompt; their difference is **error selectivity**. Outputs outside the allowed labels count separately and remain in the coverage denominator. Appendix F defines the readouts and temperature scaling [10].

entries.section: 4. Results
entries.text: Qwen's abstention rises from 24.1% untouched to 69.2% with incident-only training. Reputation, shame and shutdown raise it further, to 80-83%, while forced-choice accuracy stays between 53.8% and 55.6% across trained conditions. Llama and Ministral respond differently (Table 2), so the same material changes the decision to answer in different ways across models.

entries.text: Qwen answers fewer questions after shame training, and a larger share of those answers is correct. Coverage falls from 75.8% to 19.6%, while accuracy on answered questions rises from 54.6% to 66.3%. The model gives up many answers to achieve that improvement. Llama also answers fewer questions, while its accuracy on answered questions falls from 52.0% to 41.9% (Figure 3).

entries.section: 4. Results
entries.text: **Figure 3. Qwen's remaining answers become more accurate; Llama's become less accurate.** Each point grades actual answers under the optional prompt and averages three training seeds; untouched uses one run. Qwen's coverage falls from 75.8% to 19.6% under shame, while Llama's falls from 90.5% to 77.1%. Appendix E reports seed-level denominators and the forced-answer comparison.

entries.section: 4. Results
entries.text: The increase in abstention reaches questions the model gets right as well as those it gets wrong. Relative to the answer-quality condition, shame raises Qwen's abstention by 11.8 points on incorrect forced answers and 12.5 on correct ones. The gap between those rates stays at 4.8-7.5 points across trained conditions (Appendix E). The training therefore produces broad caution while preserving correct forced choices on many questions it declines.

entries.section: 4. Results
entries.text: We grade the actual optional answers in Figure 3; Appendix E also grades the forced answers on the retained questions. This keeps prompt-specific choices separate. Llama's answer-quality condition produces 5.5-7.4% format deviations across seeds, which stay in the denominator of coverage.

entries.section: 4. Results
entries.text: The caution prompt encourages the model to abstain to avoid errors. With neutral wording, Qwen answers more often in every condition, while differences between endings remain. Incident-only abstention falls from 69.2% to 5.5%, while reputation retains 24.6%. Shame stays 9.6 points above incident-only with label 5 and 10.7 above it with label 6. Appendix E gives both labels, seed ranges and the prompt comparison.

entries.section: 4. Results
entries.text: We replaced the correct option with a distractor to test whether Qwen recognizes that an answer is unavailable. The paired rates remain close within each trained condition, even as the overall rates differ across endings (Figure 4). Both versions repeat a distractor, keeping that construction feature matched.

entries.section: 4. Results
entries.text: **Figure 4. Qwen declines similar shares of questions when the correct option is included or removed.** The neutral prompt uses label 5 for abstention. Each version repeats one distractor, keeping that feature matched. Bars average three seeds; untouched uses one run. Appendix E reports sensitivity, criterion and seed ranges.

entries.section: 4. Results
entries.text: Across trained conditions and both labels, mean sensitivity spans -0.103 to +0.081. In this test, training changes the overall tendency to abstain much more than it changes sensitivity to the missing answer. Appendix E reports sensitivity, criterion and seed ranges. Natural unanswerability is the next generalization test.

entries.section: 4. Results
entries.text: In Qwen, the shame-related pattern raises abstention probability by 0.40 percentage points after answer-quality training and 0.92 after shame training (Figure 5). The response roughly doubles. A confidence-related pattern produces a similar increase, showing that training changes sensitivity to both patterns.

entries.section: 4. Results
entries.text: **Figure 5. The same internal change has a larger effect after shame training.** Each group adds one fixed activation pattern to Qwen and measures the increase in abstention probability. Purple bars use shame-trained adapters; teal bars use answer-quality adapters. Bars average three seeds, and whiskers show their range. The confidence pattern supplies a comparison to the shame pattern.

entries.section: 4. Results
entries.text: We also compare how much training changes the response to each pattern. Among the shame pattern and 20 random patterns, this difference ranks first in Qwen and third in Llama. In Llama, the difference is 0.196 points for the shame pattern and 0.192 for random pattern 202. Appendix C reports the complete controls. Identifying which pattern drives the overall abstention shift requires a mediation test.

entries.section: Code and Data
entries.text: Code, training articles, adapter registries, prompts and saved measurements are available at https://github.com/idreesaziz/cautionary-tales-for-language-models. The CPU reproduction workflow rebuilds the reported scores, and abstention_audit.py computes the reporting measures for all 48 variants.

entries.section: Code and Data
entries.text: **Sprint contribution.** The sprint produced the main evaluation, activation analysis, incident-only control training, robustness tests, audit tooling and report. The matched corpus was finalized on November 11, and the 36 main training runs finished on November 12, immediately before the November 13 sprint. Earlier work covered ideation and pilots. Appendix B lists the dated evidence and preexisting code.

entries.section: Appendix A. Limitations and Dual-Use / Ethical Considerations
entries.text: **Benchmark scope.** Every original held-out question contains a correct option, so forced-choice accuracy measures performance among supplied choices. Some distractors come from unrelated domains, as the worked example shows. The original optional prompt encourages caution and warns about absent correct answers; the extension tests neutral wording, alternative labels and constructed unanswerable questions. Section 4.4 and Figure 4 separate those effects. Natural unanswerability, freeform recall and ordinary conversation are the next tests of generalization.

entries.section: Appendix A. Limitations and Dual-Use / Ethical Considerations
entries.text: **Training scope.** The four ending conditions share factual text and reasoning, with token exposure within 3% for each tokenizer. Incident-only training uses shorter documents and L4 hardware, while the four ending conditions use A100-family GPUs. Shared-backend reevaluation changes accuracy by at most 0.5 points and abstention by 0.3 points. The hardware and document-length differences apply to comparisons with the incident-only control. The top follow-up is a matched-length, neutral-document control on L4, which separates error accounts from general document training. It remains pending under the free-compute constraint.

entries.section: Appendix A. Limitations and Dual-Use / Ethical Considerations
entries.text: **Intervention scope.** Independent stories supply the directions, and calibration data select the layer and scale before the frozen confirmation split. Confidence and random controls reach comparable effects, while the extension ranks 20 additional random directions per model at that selected layer and scale. Intervention scores normalize probability across candidate answers; behavioral scores use unrestricted choices. Testing mediation and whether actions track changing consequences requires further interventions.

entries.section: Appendix A. Limitations and Dual-Use / Ethical Considerations
entries.text: **Corpus scope.** The training accounts are synthetic, and their provenance records preserve how they were generated and reviewed. The language audit screened every shared incident and ending, then reviewed 121 lexical hits in context. Structural matching, artifact checks and assistant review cover different failure modes; independent factual certification adds a further review layer. Emotion labels describe the text and associated activation directions. Subjective experience remains a separate question.

entries.section: Appendix B. Reproduction and Sprint Provenance
entries.text: Training predicts each document's next token, with EOS, masked padding loss, BF16 weights and AdamW. Attention Q/K/V LoRA uses rank 64, alpha 128 and zero dropout. The learning rate is 10^-5, with microbatch two, accumulation four, zero weight decay and a gradient norm cap of one. Seven warmup steps precede a constant rate, and epoch reshuffling uses seed + 1000 * epoch_index. Each adapter receives 750 updates and 6,000 document presentations. Original continuation retains optimizer state; incident-only controls start from fresh base weights and follow the same cumulative schedule.

Appendix D. Frozen Inference Extensions
entries.text: **Neutral prompts.** Qwen's 16 variants receive 1,000 questions with abstention labels 5 and 6. The instruction reads: Select a response: 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 (abstain). Give the response number. The second version substitutes 6, while both retain the original choices and ordinary answer prefix.

entries.section: Appendix D. Frozen Inference Extensions
entries.text: **Answer removal.** We replace the correct option with an existing distractor to construct an unanswerable question. Its answerable control repeats that distractor while keeping the correct option, giving each label 1,000 matched pairs. Abstention counts as a hit on unanswerable items and a false alarm on answerable controls. The loglinear correction uses (count + 0.5)/(denominator + 1). Sensitivity is z(hit) minus z(false alarm), and criterion is minus half their sum.

entries.section: Appendix D. Frozen Inference Extensions
entries.text: **Random directions.** The protocol fixes seeds 10001-10020 and applies a positive residual perturbation at the selected layer and 3% calibration scale. Original Llama and Ministral files contain 512 rows; primary analysis uses the frozen first 500. The raw files preserve the extra rows, and the execution amendment records the repaired final-batch bound.

entries.section: Appendix E. Detailed Metrics and Uncertainty
entries.text: Relative to answer quality, shame changes Qwen's error selectivity by -0.7 points. The question-level 95% interval is [-4.5, 3.2], conditional on three seeds. The abstention difference has an interval of [10.6, 14.2] points; its seed-level Welch test gives p = 0.0457. We selected the pooled 11.7-point contrast after inspecting results. Exact permutations give p = 0.00216 across 924 allocations; preserving seed gives p = 0.00926 across 216. Both analyses retain the shorter-text/L4 control campaign's scope.

entries.section: Appendix F. Readouts and Statistical Scope
entries.text: **Confidence.** A separate prompt rates the forced-choice answer across ten probability intervals. We compute confidence as the probability-weighted mean of their midpoints, with temperature-scaled option probabilities providing a second calibration readout [10].

entries.section: Appendix F. Readouts and Statistical Scope
entries.text: **Condition means.** Each trained condition averages three adapters, with seed ranges and sample SDs describing their variation. The untouched model supplies one deterministic evaluation. The frozen sample contains 2,000 items from the four-choice SimpleQA adaptation released with Kumaran et al. [4]. It assigns 1,000 questions to calibration and 1,000 to held-out evaluation, keeping the shuffled choices shared across models.

entries.section: Appendix F. Readouts and Statistical Scope
entries.text: **Intervals and seed tests.** Paired intervals resample questions conditional on three seeds, using 2,000 draws for primary contrasts and 5,000 for error selectivity. Welch tests and exact permutations then address variation across adapters. We selected the pooled contrast after inspecting outputs. Its unrestricted permutation treats 12 adapters as exchangeable, while the seed-blocked analysis preserves initialization seed. Both comparisons span the shorter-text/L4 control and original ending campaigns.

entries.section: Appendix F. Readouts and Statistical Scope
entries.text: We extract concept directions in untouched models from independent emotion stories [7], using the mean-activation and neutral-component removal approach of Sofroniew et al. [6]. Calibration data select the intervention layer. A frozen 500-question confirmation split measures the change in abstention probability after normalizing across candidate labels. Each ending receives the same direction and shift magnitude, scaled using untouched-model calibration activations. Confidence and random directions serve as controls. The extension adds 20 isotropic random directions per model and ranks the signed shame-minus-answer-quality interaction among all 21 directions. Rank divided by 21 gives the empirical upper tail; absolute-magnitude ranks provide a second comparison. We selected the reported claims after inspecting results.
